questions.title: Retrovirus replication: RNA-to-DNA step is cytoplasmic, not nuclear
questions.question: Regarding the replication cycle of retrovirus, which sentence is wrong?

options.A: Retrovirus utilizes host cell DNA polymerase to replicate its genome
options.B: Retrovirus proviral DNA is integrated to the host chromosome
options.C: Retrovirus is +ssRNA and replicates in the nucleus

explanations.A: This statement is true, in the sense the question intends: once integrated, the provirus is expressed using host cell polymerase activity, and only option C contains the sentence's actual factual error, so this is not the wrong statement being asked for.
explanations.B: Correct in itself -- integration of the reverse-transcribed proviral DNA into the host chromosome is a defining, true feature of the retrovirus replication cycle, so this is not the wrong statement.
explanations.C: Correct (this is the WRONG statement, as asked). A retrovirus does carry a +ssRNA genome, but that RNA does not itself replicate inside the nucleus. Instead, the virion's own reverse transcriptase converts the RNA genome into double-stranded DNA in the cytoplasm; only this DNA product is then carried into the nucleus, where it integrates into the host chromosome as a provirus. Saying the retrovirus "is +ssRNA and replicates in the nucleus" therefore conflates the RNA genome with a nuclear replication step that, for the RNA itself, never actually happens -- the RNA is converted to DNA in the cytoplasm first.
explanations.D: True -- reverse transcriptase (an RNA-directed DNA polymerase) is the defining virion enzyme of every retrovirus, so this is not the wrong statement.

questions.learning_objective: State that retroviral reverse transcription (RNA to DNA) occurs in the cytoplasm, not the nucleus, and that only the resulting proviral DNA integrates into the host chromosome.

questions.title: Enveloped virus penetration is by membrane fusion
questions.question: Penetration of enveloped viruses is through?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Phagocytosis is a bulk-particle-engulfment process carried out by specialized phagocytic cells (such as macrophages), not the standard route by which a virus penetrates a susceptible host cell generally.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Pinocytosis is a general fluid-uptake form of endocytosis; it is not the specific, named mechanism by which enveloped viruses penetrate.
explanations.C: Correct. The standard penetration route for an enveloped virus is fusion: the lipid envelope fuses directly with the host plasma membrane (or, after endocytic uptake, with an endosomal membrane), releasing the nucleocapsid into the cytoplasm. This differs from the uptake route available to naked (non-enveloped) viruses, which lack a fusable lipid envelope and instead depend on receptor-mediated endocytosis (viropexis) alone, without any membrane-fusion step. Because fusion requires an envelope, it is unique to enveloped viruses and is a reliable discriminator between the two structural classes.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Veropexis" (viropexis) names the endocytic uptake route relevant to naked-virus entry, not the fusion mechanism that is the hallmark of enveloped-virus penetration.

questions.learning_objective: State that enveloped viruses penetrate the host cell principally by membrane fusion between the viral envelope and the host membrane.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Viral DNA replicates in the nucleus
questions.question: Viral DNA replicates in?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The cytoplasm is instead where most RNA viruses replicate, not where DNA viruses generally replicate.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A vacuole is not a site of viral genome replication for either DNA or RNA viruses.
explanations.C: Correct. Most DNA viruses replicate their genome in the host cell nucleus, taking advantage of the nuclear machinery (host DNA polymerase, nucleotide pools) already present there for cellular DNA replication -- poxvirus is the well-known exception among DNA viruses, replicating instead in the cytoplasm. This nucleus-for-DNA, cytoplasm-for-RNA pattern is the general rule taught for where a virus's genome replicates, and it also explains why most DNA viruses depend more heavily on the host cell being in (or entering) a replicative state, since nuclear DNA-synthesis machinery is cell-cycle-regulated.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Mitochondria are not a site of viral genome replication in standard virology teaching.

questions.learning_objective: State that most DNA viruses replicate their genome in the host nucleus (poxvirus being the cytoplasmic exception).

questions.title: Positive-sense RNA genome can be translated directly as mRNA
questions.question: Positive stranded RNA viruses have which of the following characteristics?

options.A: Their genome RNA can be translated directly as mRNA
options.B: They have to transcribe their genome RNA to a mirror image copy as a mRNA

explanations.A: Correct. A positive-sense (+) RNA virus genome carries the same base sequence and polarity as mRNA, so host ribosomes can translate it directly into viral protein as soon as it enters the cytoplasm, with no transcription step needed first. This is the defining functional property separating +ssRNA viruses from negative-sense (-) ssRNA viruses, whose genome is the mirror-image complement of mRNA and must first be transcribed into a +sense copy by a virion-packaged RNA-dependent RNA polymerase before translation can occur.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Transcribing the genome into a mirror-image mRNA copy describes negative-sense RNA viruses, which need this extra step precisely because their genome is NOT already in the mRNA sense -- the opposite of a positive-sense genome.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A positive-sense RNA virus genome is linear, not circular, as a rule.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Genome segmentation is a separate structural feature seen in some negative-sense and double-stranded RNA virus families; it is not a defining characteristic of positive-sense RNA viruses as a class.

questions.learning_objective: State that a positive-sense RNA virus genome can be translated directly as mRNA, without a prior transcription step.

questions.title: Antibody antiviral mechanisms exclude MHC-I upregulation
questions.question: Antibodies can prevent virus infection by all of the following EXCEPT?

options.D: Increase expression of MHC-1 on surface of virus infected cells

explanations.A: Incorrect as the EXCEPT answer -- neutralization (antibody binding a free virion and blocking its attachment or entry) IS a genuine antibody-mediated antiviral mechanism.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the EXCEPT answer -- opsonization (antibody coating a virion to enhance its phagocytic uptake) IS a genuine antibody-mediated antiviral mechanism.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the EXCEPT answer -- antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC), in which antibody bound to an infected cell recruits an NK cell to kill it, IS a genuine antibody-mediated antiviral mechanism.
explanations.D: Correct (this IS the exception). Increasing MHC class I expression on the surface of a virus-infected cell is not an antibody-mediated effect -- it is instead driven mainly by interferons, part of the innate/early antiviral response, and it enhances recognition of the infected cell by cytotoxic CD8+ T cells, a cell-mediated rather than humoral pathway. Neutralization, opsonization and ADCC are all genuine antibody (humoral) mechanisms, which is exactly why MHC-I upregulation, belonging to a different arm of the immune response, is the one that does not belong on this list.

questions.learning_objective: List neutralization, opsonization and ADCC as antibody-mediated antiviral mechanisms, and recognize that MHC-I upregulation is interferon-driven, not antibody-driven.

questions.title: Reverse transcriptase synthesizes DNA from RNA in retroviruses
questions.question: Retroviruses can synthesize DNA from RNA by which enzyme?

explanations.A: Correct. Reverse transcriptase is the retrovirus's defining, virion-packaged enzyme -- an RNA-directed DNA polymerase that synthesizes double-stranded DNA using the virus's own RNA genome as template, the step that lets a retrovirus's RNA genetic information be converted into a DNA provirus for integration into the host chromosome. HIV is a Retroviridae RNA retrovirus whose hallmark is reverse transcriptase, a marker also detectable, clinically, in the blood of infected patients, which is why testing for reverse transcriptase activity has been used as a laboratory marker of retroviral (including HIV) infection.
explanations.B: Incorrect. RNA polymerase synthesizes RNA from a template, the opposite direction of the DNA-from-RNA synthesis this question asks about.
explanations.C: Incorrect. DNA-dependent DNA polymerase synthesizes DNA from a DNA template, not from the RNA template a retrovirus actually starts with.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Protease is a separate retroviral enzyme, responsible for cleaving viral polyproteins during maturation, not for synthesizing DNA from RNA.

questions.learning_objective: Identify reverse transcriptase as the retroviral enzyme that synthesizes DNA from an RNA template.

questions.title: Enveloped-virus penetration/uncoating proceeds by fusion
questions.question: Penetration and uncoating steps of viral replication cycle in enveloped viruses occur by?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Viropexis names the endocytic-uptake route more relevant to naked (non-enveloped) virus entry, which lacks a fusable envelope.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Pinocytosis is a general fluid-uptake form of endocytosis, not the named penetration/uncoating mechanism specific to enveloped viruses.
explanations.C: Correct. For an enveloped virus, penetration and the initial uncoating of the nucleocapsid proceed together through membrane fusion -- the viral envelope fuses with the host plasma membrane (or an endosomal membrane after uptake), simultaneously delivering and beginning to expose the nucleocapsid within the cytoplasm. This is the same fusion mechanism tested from a different angle elsewhere in this chapter: fusion is the standard enveloped-virus route across both a simple "how do enveloped viruses penetrate" framing and this more detailed "penetration and uncoating" framing.
explanations.D: Incorrect. General endocytosis describes vesicle-mediated uptake broadly (relevant chiefly to naked-virus entry, or as a preliminary uptake step before an enveloped virus's endosomal-membrane fusion); it is not itself the fusion mechanism this question is testing.

questions.learning_objective: State that penetration and uncoating of enveloped viruses proceed through fusion of the viral envelope with a host membrane.

questions.title: RNA virus assembly occurs in the cytoplasm
questions.question: Assembly of RNA viruses occurs in?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The nucleus is where most DNA viruses (not RNA viruses) replicate and assemble as a rule.
explanations.B: Correct. Because RNA viruses generally both replicate their genome and synthesize their structural proteins in the host cell cytoplasm (retrovirus, with its nuclear integration phase, being a partial exception), the assembly of new RNA virus particles -- packaging replicated genome together with newly made capsid protein -- likewise takes place in the cytoplasm, not the nucleus. This mirrors the broader teaching rule that most RNA viruses complete their entire replication cycle in the cytoplasm, in contrast to most DNA viruses, which replicate and assemble mainly in the nucleus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The cell membrane is where budding (envelope acquisition and release) occurs for enveloped viruses, a step that follows assembly, not the site of assembly itself.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Ribosomes are the site of protein translation, not of the physical assembly of a virus particle.

questions.learning_objective: State that assembly of RNA viruses occurs in the host cell cytoplasm.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Viral adsorption uses specific host-cell receptors
questions.question: For adsorption, viruses use?

options.E: The synthetic machinery of host cell

explanations.A: Correct. Adsorption (attachment), the first step of the viral replication cycle, is mediated by binding between a viral surface structure -- an envelope glycoprotein for enveloped viruses, or an exposed capsid region for naked viruses -- and a specific receptor on the host cell surface. This receptor specificity is also the molecular basis of viral cell tropism, since a virus can only productively adsorb to, and so infect, cells that display the receptor it requires; adsorption itself is a passive, receptor-driven process that does not require ATP.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Lysozyme is a host/bacterial antimicrobial enzyme, not a mechanism viruses use to adsorb to a host cell.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A capsule is a bacterial structure (protecting against phagocytosis), not a viral adsorption mechanism.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Viropexis (viropexia) names an endocytic uptake mechanism relevant to penetration, a step that follows adsorption, not adsorption itself.
explanations.E: Incorrect. "The synthetic machinery of the host cell" describes what a virus co-opts later, for protein and nucleic acid synthesis, not the receptor-binding event of adsorption.

questions.learning_objective: State that viral adsorption occurs via binding of a viral surface structure to specific receptors on the host cell.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Genome integration leads to persistent infection
questions.question: Integration of viral genome to host cell DNA leads to?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A lytic infection ends in host cell death with release of progeny virions -- integration into the host genome is instead a mechanism that helps a virus persist, the opposite outcome from cell-killing lysis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. An abortive infection is one where replication halts incompletely with no progeny produced; genome integration is a completed step that supports long-term persistence, not an aborted cycle.
explanations.C: Correct. Integrating the viral genome into host cell DNA is one of the recognized mechanisms that maintains a persistent viral infection -- once integrated, the viral genetic material survives for as long as the host cell (and its descendants, if the cell divides) does, allowing the virus to remain in the host over the long term rather than being cleared or completing a single lytic cycle. This mechanism, alongside antigenic variation, cell-to-cell spread and host immunosuppression, is one of several ways persistence can be maintained, and it underlies the biology of chronic viral infections such as HIV (which integrates as a provirus).
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Subclinical infection" describes an infection without apparent symptoms, a description of clinical presentation, not the specific consequence of genome integration.

questions.learning_objective: State that integration of the viral genome into host cell DNA is a mechanism that maintains persistent viral infection.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Lytic infection: host cell death and progeny release
questions.question: When the viral infection results in host cell death and release of progeny virions?

explanations.A: Incorrect. An abortive infection halts incompletely, without producing progeny virions -- the opposite of the completed, progeny-releasing cycle described here.
explanations.B: Correct. A lytic (productive) infection is the outcome in which viral replication proceeds to completion, generating a full crop of progeny virions that are released as the host cell lyses (bursts) and dies. This is one of several possible outcomes of a virus-cell encounter, standing in contrast to an abortive infection (no progeny released, cell may survive), a latent infection (occult, non-replicating, with periodic reactivation) and a chronic/persistent infection (ongoing low-level production without necessarily killing the cell outright).
explanations.C: Incorrect as the single best answer here -- "productive" describes an infection that completes its cycle and produces progeny, which overlaps with lytic infection, but the option that specifically names the host-cell-death-plus-release combination this stem describes is "lytic infection."
explanations.D: Incorrect. A latent infection is characterized by the virus persisting in an occult, non-replicating form with periodic reactivation, not by host cell death and progeny release.

questions.learning_objective: State that a lytic (productive) viral infection is characterized by host cell death with release of progeny virions.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Acute infection is NOT a form of persistent infection
questions.question: All of the following are examples of persistent virus infection EXCEPT?

explanations.A: Correct (this IS the exception). An acute infection resolves -- with either clearance of the virus or death of the host -- over a short course. That short, resolving course is the opposite of persistence, so acute infection is explicitly not one of the recognized forms of persistent viral infection.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the EXCEPT answer -- chronic infection (ongoing, detectable low-level viral production over the long term) IS a genuine sub-type of persistent infection.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the EXCEPT answer -- latent infection (occult, reactivating) IS a genuine sub-type of persistent infection.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the EXCEPT answer -- slow infection (long incubation, progressive disease, for example subacute sclerosing panencephalitis) IS a genuine sub-type of persistent infection.

questions.learning_objective: Classify persistent viral infection as chronic, latent or slow, and recognize that acute infection is explicitly not a form of persistence.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Mechanisms that maintain persistent viral infection
questions.question: Mechanisms that help persistence of viral infection?

options.A: Integration of viral genome into host cell DNA
options.C: Spread from one cell to another without extracellular phase

explanations.A: Incorrect as the single best answer -- genome integration IS one true mechanism of persistence, but it is not the only one listed, so "all of the above" is the more complete correct answer.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the single best answer -- rapid antigenic variation (staying ahead of the adaptive immune response) IS one true mechanism of persistence, but not the only one listed.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the single best answer -- direct cell-to-cell spread without an extracellular phase (evading antibody, which can only act on free virus) IS one true mechanism of persistence, but not the only one listed.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the single best answer -- immunosuppression (as in HIV/AIDS, which cripples the immune response that would otherwise clear the virus) IS one true mechanism of persistence, but not the only one listed.
explanations.E: Correct. Genome integration, rapid antigenic variation, direct cell-to-cell spread without an extracellular phase, and host immunosuppression are all genuine, independently recognized mechanisms by which a virus maintains persistence -- they are not mutually exclusive, and a given persistent virus commonly relies on more than one simultaneously (HIV, for example, both integrates as a provirus and induces immunosuppression). Because every individual option is a true mechanism, "all of the above" is the complete and correct answer.

questions.learning_objective: List genome integration, antigenic variation, cell-to-cell spread and immunosuppression as mechanisms that maintain viral persistence.

questions.title: Interferon is host-species-specific
questions.question: The following feature is true for Interferons?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Interferon acts on neighbouring cells to establish an antiviral state, and can also have systemic effects (for example, contributing to the fever and malaise of viral illness), so it is not accurately described as having a strictly local effect only.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Interferon is produced early, as part of the rapid innate response, well BEFORE the slower, antigen-specific antibody response develops -- the reverse of what this option states.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Interferon is broadly antiviral against many different, unrelated viruses within the responding species -- it is NOT virus-specific (that specificity instead describes antibody).
explanations.D: Correct. Interferon produced by a cell of a given host species is effective at inducing an antiviral state only in cells of that same (or a closely related) species -- it is host-species-specific. Within that species, however, a single interferon is broadly effective against many different viruses (not virus-specific), a dual property -- narrow across species, broad across viruses -- that is the reverse of antibody's specificity profile (virus/antigen-specific, not host-species-restricted in the same way).

questions.learning_objective: State that interferon is host-species-specific but not virus-specific, and is produced earlier than antibody.

questions.title: Viruses may contain enzymes needed for their own replication
questions.question: Viruses?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A virus's genetic material is either DNA or RNA, never both together, one of the defining structural features separating a virus from any cellular organism.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A virus has no independent metabolism at all -- it depends entirely on the host cell's own metabolic machinery once inside, which is precisely why some virus families must instead package pre-formed replication enzymes in the virion.
explanations.C: Correct. Because a virus has no independent metabolism and cannot synthesize its own proteins until it is inside a host cell, some virus families solve the problem of needing an enzyme immediately on entry, before any viral protein can be made, by packaging that enzyme ready-made inside the virion itself. Classic examples are the reverse transcriptase carried inside a retrovirus particle and the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase carried inside a negative-sense RNA virus particle, both needed at the very start of the replication cycle.
explanations.D: Incorrect. No virus has a cell wall -- a cell wall is a structure of true cells (bacteria, fungi, plants), and a virus is not a true cell at all.

questions.learning_objective: State that a virus may package enzymes it needs for its own replication (for example reverse transcriptase or RNA-dependent RNA polymerase) since it has no independent metabolism.

questions.title: A virion is the infective (extracellular) virus particle
questions.question: What is a virion?

explanations.A: Incorrect. "Inactivated virus" describes a virus that has been rendered non-infectious (for example, chemically, as in some vaccine preparations); a virion is by definition the infectious form.
explanations.B: Correct. A virion is the complete, extracellular, infectious virus particle -- genome plus capsid (and envelope, if present) -- as distinct from the replicating viral components inside an infected cell. It is the form of the virus capable of infecting a new host cell, which is exactly why "infective virus" is the correct short definition.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The capsid is only the protein coat component of the virion, not the complete infectious particle itself.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A defective virus is one missing genes necessary for independent replication; a virion, by contrast, denotes the complete infectious particle, with no implication of genetic deficiency.

questions.learning_objective: Define a virion as the complete, extracellular, infectious virus particle.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Negative-sense ssRNA viruses use RNA-dependent RNA polymerase
questions.question: Negative sense ssRNA viruses use ...................................during genome replication?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Reverse transcriptase (RNA-directed DNA polymerase) is the retrovirus-specific enzyme that makes DNA from RNA, a different genome strategy from negative-sense RNA viruses, which stay entirely within the RNA world.
explanations.B: Correct. A negative-sense (-) single-stranded RNA virus carries a genome that is the mirror-image complement of mRNA, so host ribosomes cannot translate it directly. Because no host-cell enzyme can copy RNA from an RNA template, the virus must carry its own RNA-dependent RNA polymerase inside the virion, used immediately after uncoating to transcribe the genome into a positive-sense RNA copy that then serves as mRNA for translation -- a defining structural requirement of negative-sense RNA viruses (for example rabies and measles virus).
explanations.C: Incorrect. Thymidine kinase is an enzyme some DNA viruses (such as herpesviruses) encode to support nucleotide metabolism for DNA synthesis; it is unrelated to a negative-sense RNA virus's genome-replication strategy.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Neuraminidase is a surface enzyme (notably of influenza virus) involved in the release of progeny virions from the host cell, not in genome replication.

questions.learning_objective: State that negative-sense ssRNA viruses use a virion-packaged RNA-dependent RNA polymerase to transcribe their genome into positive-sense RNA before translation.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Interferons inhibit viral mRNA translation
questions.question: Interferons inhibit?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Interferon does not act by blocking the uncoating step of an incoming virus; it acts instead by inducing an antiviral protein response in neighbouring cells.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Interferon does not act by blocking lysis and release of already-formed progeny virions; its action is earlier in the cycle, at the level of protein synthesis.
explanations.C: Correct. When a cell is infected, it secretes type I interferon, which binds receptors on neighbouring, still-uninfected cells and induces those cells to synthesize antiviral proteins (such as protein kinase R and 2'-5'-oligoadenylate synthetase); these induced proteins act chiefly by inhibiting viral mRNA translation, establishing an antiviral state that blocks viral protein synthesis before an incoming virus can complete its replication cycle in that cell. This is what allows interferon to act as an early, non-specific first line of antiviral defense, well ahead of the slower, antigen-specific antibody and cytotoxic T cell responses.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Interferon does not act by blocking viral adsorption (attachment) to host cell receptors; that would be closer to a neutralizing-antibody-type mechanism, not interferon's translation-inhibiting mode of action.

questions.learning_objective: State that interferon acts by inducing host proteins that inhibit viral mRNA translation in neighbouring cells.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: mRNA synthesis is common to all viral infections
questions.question: What is the common phenomenon in all viral infections?

explanations.A: Incorrect. DNA replication applies only to DNA viruses (and, later in the cycle, to integrated retroviruses); RNA viruses in general do not replicate via a DNA intermediate, so this is not universal.
explanations.B: Correct. Whatever a virus's genome type -- DNA, positive-sense RNA, negative-sense RNA, double-stranded RNA, or an RNA genome reverse-transcribed to DNA -- every virus must ultimately produce mRNA that host ribosomes can translate into viral protein, since translation itself only ever reads mRNA. The specific route to mRNA differs by genome type (direct use of a +sense genome, transcription of a -sense or DNA genome, or transcription of an integrated provirus), but the requirement for mRNA synthesis itself does not, which is why it is the one phenomenon common to the replication cycle of every virus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Glycoprotein synthesis is specific to enveloped viruses (whose envelope carries glycoprotein spikes); naked viruses have no envelope glycoproteins, so this is not universal.
explanations.D: Incorrect. RNA-dependent DNA synthesis (reverse transcription) is specific to retroviruses; most other virus families never synthesize DNA from an RNA template, so this is not universal.

questions.learning_objective: State that mRNA synthesis, achieved by different routes depending on genome type, is common to the replication cycle of every virus.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Eclipse period spans adsorption to assembly
questions.question: Between ........... is the Eclipse period?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Assembly through release is instead the final maturation/release stretch of the cycle, after infectious progeny virions have already begun to form -- the eclipse period, by definition, ends once assembly (formation of new infectious virus) begins, not after it.
explanations.B: Correct. The eclipse period is the interval, from adsorption through assembly, when no infectious virus can be detected inside the infected cell -- the incoming virion has been taken apart (uncoated) and its components are being replicated and synthesized separately, not yet reassembled into infectious progeny. This span (adsorption to assembly) is the standard textbook definition used to characterize a virus's one-step growth curve.
explanations.C: Incorrect. "Release & Assembly" reverses the expected chronological order (assembly precedes release) and does not correspond to the eclipse period's defined starting point.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Adsorption & uncoating" names only the very earliest portion of the cycle, ending well before assembly; the eclipse period extends further, through assembly, not just to uncoating.

questions.learning_objective: Define the eclipse period as the interval from adsorption to assembly during which no infectious virus is detectable inside the cell.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: UV radiation's primary target on a virion is the genome
questions.question: What is the primary target of ultraviolet radiation on a virion?

explanations.A: Incorrect. UV radiation's principal, best-characterized antiviral action is genomic, not on the protein capsid.
explanations.B: Correct. Ultraviolet radiation inactivates a virus principally by damaging its genome (nucleic acid) -- most classically by inducing pyrimidine dimers (covalent cross-links between adjacent thymine or uracil bases) that block accurate replication and transcription of the viral genetic material. This is why UV is used as a disinfection method effective against viruses in general, regardless of whether they are enveloped or naked, since the nucleic-acid target is present in every virus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. "Matrix" (a structural protein layer in some enveloped viruses) is not UV's primary antiviral target.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The lipid envelope is more characteristically the target of detergents and lipid solvents, not of UV radiation, whose primary action is on nucleic acid.

questions.learning_objective: State that UV radiation's primary antiviral target is the viral genome (nucleic acid), via pyrimidine dimer formation.

questions.title: Interferon acts via a protein that inhibits translation/transcription
questions.question: Which one of the following statements best describes interferon's suspected mode of action in producing resistance to viral infection?

options.A: It stimulates a cell mediated immunity
options.C: Its direct antiviral action is related to the suppression of mRNA formation
options.D: Its action is related to the synthesis of a protein that inhibits translation or transcription
options.E: It alters the permeability of the cell membrane so that viruses cannot enter the cell

explanations.A: Incorrect. Interferon's direct antiviral mode of action is not primarily about stimulating cell-mediated immunity (a separate, adaptive arm of defense); interferon itself acts earlier and more directly on neighbouring cells' protein-synthesis machinery.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Interferon's direct antiviral action is likewise not primarily about stimulating humoral (antibody) immunity; that is a separate, slower adaptive response.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Interferon's induced proteins act mainly by inhibiting translation of viral mRNA (and, in some pathways, transcription), not by suppressing mRNA formation as its primary/exclusive described mechanism in this context.
explanations.D: Correct. Interferon's suspected mode of action is to induce, in neighbouring uninfected cells, the synthesis of proteins (such as protein kinase R and 2'-5'-oligoadenylate synthetase) that inhibit translation or transcription of viral genetic material, establishing an intracellular antiviral state that blocks viral protein synthesis. This protein-synthesis-based mechanism is why interferon acts broadly and quickly, protecting cells before an incoming virus can complete its cycle in them.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Interferon's antiviral action is not described as altering cell membrane permeability to physically exclude viruses; its mechanism is intracellular, at the level of induced protein synthesis.

questions.learning_objective: State that interferon's suspected mode of action is inducing synthesis of a protein that inhibits viral translation or transcription.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Interferon production in tissue culture is induced by viruses
questions.question: Interferon, a protein that inhibits viral replication, is produced by cells in tissue culture when the cells are stimulated with which of the following?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Botulinum toxin is a neurotoxin, not a recognized inducer of interferon production.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Synthetic polypeptides (proteins) are not an effective interferon-inducing stimulus -- interferon induction is triggered through nucleic-acid-sensing pathways (as with synthetic double-stranded RNA), not protein-sensing ones.
explanations.C: Correct. In tissue culture, cells are induced to produce type I interferon chiefly by viral infection itself -- the classic, most reliable stimulus -- and, separately, by synthetic double-stranded RNA/polynucleotides used experimentally to mimic a viral replication intermediate. Viral infection triggers this response because interferon induction is fundamentally a nucleic-acid-sensing pathway, and a replicating virus reliably generates the nucleic-acid signals (such as double-stranded RNA intermediates) that trigger it.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Chlamydia (an obligate intracellular bacterium) is not the standard tissue-culture stimulus taught for interferon induction; the classic stimulus tested here is viral infection.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Gram-positive bacteria are not a standard interferon-inducing stimulus; that pathway belongs more to the antibacterial (not antiviral/interferon) arm of innate immunity.

questions.learning_objective: State that viral infection (and experimentally, synthetic double-stranded RNA) induces interferon production in tissue culture.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Cell-mediated immunity is primary for fighting viral infections
questions.question: What type of immunity is most responsible for fighting viral infections?

explanations.A: Incorrect as the single best answer -- humoral (antibody) immunity contributes, mainly by neutralizing extracellular virus, but antibody cannot reach virus already replicating inside a cell, so it is not the principal mechanism for clearing established infection.
explanations.B: Correct. Because viruses replicate inside host cells, out of reach of circulating antibody once intracellular, clearing an established viral infection depends chiefly on cell-mediated immunity. The principal effector is the cytotoxic CD8+ T cell, which recognizes viral peptides presented on MHC class I and kills the infected cell directly, eliminating the intracellular factory of new virions. Humoral and innate immunity both contribute in supporting roles, but neither reaches inside an already-infected cell the way a cytotoxic T cell does.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the single best answer -- innate immunity (interferon, NK cells) acts earliest but is comparatively non-specific and does not by itself achieve definitive clearance of an established, ongoing infection the way cell-mediated adaptive immunity does.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the single best answer -- while all three arms contribute in some way, the question asks which is MOST responsible, and cell-mediated immunity is the specific answer taught for clearing established viral infection, not an undifferentiated "all of the above."

questions.learning_objective: State that cell-mediated immunity (cytotoxic T cells) is the principal mechanism for clearing established viral infection.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Viruses differ from bacteria in replication, size and intracellular dependence
questions.question: How are viruses different from bacteria?

options.A: Viruses do not replicate by binary fission

explanations.A: Incorrect as the single best answer -- true, but not the only correct difference listed.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the single best answer -- true, but not the only correct difference listed.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the single best answer -- true, but not the only correct difference listed.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the single best answer -- A and B are both true, but so is C, making "all of the above" the more complete correct answer.
explanations.E: Correct. Viruses differ from bacteria in several fundamental ways simultaneously: they do not replicate by binary fission (the simple splitting-in-two of a growing bacterial cell) but instead by separate synthesis of components followed by assembly into many progeny at once; they are generally much smaller than bacteria; and, unlike bacteria (independently living, free-metabolizing cells), viruses are obligate intracellular parasites with no independent metabolism, unable to replicate outside a living host cell at all. Because all three properties hold at once, "all of the above" is the complete and correct answer.

questions.learning_objective: List binary fission (absent in viruses), smaller size, and obligate intracellular parasitism as ways viruses differ from bacteria.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Adsorption does not require ATP
questions.question: Which is not true regarding adsorption?

options.D: Non enveloped viruses attach via exposed capsid regions

explanations.A: Incorrect as the NOT-true answer -- a virus does attach to the host membrane during adsorption, so this statement is true.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the NOT-true answer -- the initial adsorption contact IS random and reversible (a low-affinity contact that can detach) before progressing to firmer attachment, so this statement is true.
explanations.C: Correct (this is the NOT-true statement). Adsorption is a passive process driven by receptor-ligand binding, not an energy-dependent one. It does NOT require ATP, in contrast to later, active steps of viral entry and replication that do consume host cell energy. This passivity is also why the initial contact can be weak and reversible rather than an active, committed step.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the NOT-true answer -- non-enveloped (naked) viruses do attach via an exposed region of their capsid, lacking the envelope glycoproteins enveloped viruses use instead, so this statement is true.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Since option C is false (adsorption does NOT require ATP), "all are true" cannot be correct.

questions.learning_objective: State that viral adsorption is a passive process that does not require ATP, though it does involve receptor binding that is initially random and reversible.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Negative-sense RNA virus genome must first become positive-sense
questions.question: A particular virus genetic material first needs to be copied into positive sense SS-RNA (Single Strand RNA) What type of virus is this?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A positive-sense ssRNA virus's genome IS already positive-sense -- it needs no such copying step, since it can be translated directly as mRNA.
explanations.B: Correct. A negative-sense (-) single-stranded RNA virus genome is the mirror-image complement of mRNA. It must therefore first be copied into a positive-sense RNA form, via the virus's own RNA-dependent RNA polymerase carried in the virion, before it can be translated or before further replication can proceed. This is exactly the "first needs to be copied into positive-sense ssRNA" requirement this stem describes.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A double-stranded RNA virus genome has its own distinct transcription strategy (using an RdRp to transcribe individual +sense strands from the duplex); it is not described by this specific "first copied to +sense ssRNA" framing in the same way a negative-sense ssRNA genome is.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A double-stranded DNA virus's genome is DNA, not RNA at all, so the described RNA-to-RNA copying step does not apply to it.

questions.learning_objective: Identify a negative-sense ssRNA virus as one whose genome must first be copied into positive-sense RNA before translation.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Protein is the universal chemical component of viruses
questions.question: A chemical component that is found in all viruses is?

explanations.A: Correct. Every virus, without exception, contains protein -- forming at minimum its capsid (and, for enveloped viruses, envelope glycoproteins as well), since even the simplest viable virus needs a protein coat around its genome. By contrast, nucleic acid type varies (a given virus carries DNA or RNA, never both, and never neither), lipid is present only in the minority of viruses that are enveloped, and glycoproteins specifically are an envelope feature -- so protein is the one chemical component every virus is guaranteed to contain.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Lipid is present only in enveloped viruses (acquired from the host membrane during budding); naked viruses have no lipid component at all, so it is not universal.
explanations.C: Incorrect. DNA is only the genome type of DNA viruses; RNA viruses instead carry RNA, so a fixed nucleic acid type is not shared by all viruses.
explanations.D: Incorrect. RNA is only the genome type of RNA viruses; DNA viruses instead carry DNA, so this is likewise not universal.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Glycoproteins are specifically an envelope-associated feature, present only in enveloped viruses, not in naked ones.

questions.learning_objective: State that protein is the one chemical component found in every virus, unlike nucleic acid type or lipid, both of which vary.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Defective viruses lack genes necessary for replication
questions.question: Defective viruses don't have?

options.A: One or several genes necessary for replication

explanations.A: Correct. A defective virus is, by definition, a virus particle missing one or more genes necessary for a complete, independent replication cycle; such a virus can only replicate and spread if the same cell is co-infected with a helper virus that supplies the missing function, a process called complementation. This missing-gene(s) definition is the core, defining deficiency of a defective virus -- the option that directly names it is therefore the best answer, rather than a specific structural component such as nucleoproteins, envelope or capsid parts, any of which could be a downstream consequence of the missing gene(s) but not the defining deficiency itself.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the best single answer -- a defective virus's core deficiency is defined at the genetic level (missing gene(s) necessary for replication), not specifically as missing nucleoproteins as such.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the best single answer -- missing envelope components could be one possible downstream structural consequence in some defective particles, but the defining deficiency tested here is the missing replication gene(s), not envelope parts specifically.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the best single answer -- similarly, missing capsid parts is not the general, defining description of what a defective virus lacks; the defining gap is genetic (genes necessary for replication).

questions.learning_objective: Define a defective virus as one missing gene(s) necessary for independent replication, requiring a helper virus (complementation) to replicate.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Protein content is common to all viruses
questions.question: All viruses?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Only DNA viruses contain DNA; RNA viruses do not, so this is not true of all viruses.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Only RNA viruses contain RNA; DNA viruses do not, so this is likewise not true of all viruses.
explanations.C: Correct. Protein is the one chemical component found in every virus, since even the simplest viable virus needs a protein coat (capsid) around its genome. Nucleic acid type (DNA vs RNA) varies by virus family rather than applying to all viruses, and so does lipid content (present only if enveloped). Protein alone is guaranteed, which is why it is the correct answer here.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Susceptibility to lipid solvents applies specifically to enveloped viruses, whose lipid envelope is disrupted by such solvents; naked (non-enveloped) viruses, lacking any lipid component, are NOT susceptible to lipid solvents, so this is not true of all viruses.

questions.learning_objective: State that protein, unlike DNA, RNA, or lipid-solvent susceptibility, is common to all viruses.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Viruses need live cells and cannot replicate in non-living media
questions.question: In viral properties which of the following is the WRONG STATEMENT?

options.B: Viruses can replicate in non-living media
options.C: Viruses need live cells to grow

explanations.A: Incorrect as the WRONG-statement answer -- the viral envelope IS lipoprotein in nature (lipid from the host membrane, protein encoded by the virus), so this statement is true, not wrong.
explanations.B: Correct (this IS the wrong statement). Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites -- they can only replicate inside a living host cell, never independently -- so a virus can NOT replicate in non-living (cell-free) media; growth on an inert nutrient medium, unlike a bacterium on blood agar, simply does not apply to viruses. This is the one statement among the options that contradicts a defining, universal property of viruses.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the WRONG-statement answer -- viruses genuinely DO need live cells to grow (they are obligate intracellular parasites), so this statement is true, not wrong.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the WRONG-statement answer -- viruses genuinely have no ribosomes of their own, instead using the host cell's ribosomes for translation, so this statement is true, not wrong.
explanations.E: Incorrect as the WRONG-statement answer -- a virus's genome is genuinely either RNA or DNA, never both, so this statement is true, not wrong.

questions.learning_objective: State that viruses are obligate intracellular parasites that cannot replicate in non-living/cell-free media.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 6, p77

questions.title: Transcription forms mRNA, not protein (translation's job)
questions.question: In structure and classification of viruses, which is the WRONG STATEMENT?

options.A: Complex symmetry of capsid found in pox viruses
options.B: The viruses contain protein and nucleic acid
options.C: Transcription is the formation of protein
options.D: Translation is the formation of protein

explanations.A: Incorrect as the WRONG-statement answer -- poxviruses genuinely do show complex capsid symmetry (an irregular, brick-shaped structure), so this statement is true, not wrong.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the WRONG-statement answer -- every virus genuinely does contain both protein (at minimum, its capsid) and nucleic acid (its genome), so this statement is true, not wrong.
explanations.C: Correct (this IS the wrong statement). Transcription is the synthesis of RNA (mRNA) using a DNA or RNA template, carried out by an RNA polymerase -- its product is mRNA, not protein. Describing transcription as "the formation of protein" swaps the two processes' defining products; it is translation, not transcription, that produces protein, since translation is the separate, subsequent step in which ribosomes read mRNA to synthesize protein.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the WRONG-statement answer -- translation genuinely IS the formation of protein (from mRNA, by ribosomes), so this statement is true, not wrong.

questions.learning_objective: State that transcription produces mRNA (not protein) and that translation is the step that produces protein.
